title: Indie hacking after the job honeymoon: motivation, burnout and what to build next
summary: Dagobert reflects on three months at a job, why it never fully satisfies him, and how comparing himself to lifestyle-focused indie hackers fed his burnout. He decides to build things that help indies and freelancers, reviews why Logology failed, and weighs pivots and a course update.

principles.text: Build what comes from inside and helps people; that is what makes work meaningful.
principles.quote: really what makes it meaningful is that it comes from like inside like it's like really something that I want to give

principles.text: Know your real driver. Copying other indie hackers' lifestyle goals led to burnout; his driver is contributing and supporting others.
principles.quote: my driver is different my driver is more like arid and my driver is more like I want to contribute I want to help I want to support others

principles.text: Lower your expectations of a job and you perform better at it.
principles.quote: I actually feel way better at this job now I'm like you know I'm way more productive because I don't expect too much from it

principles.text: Serving people who can't pay without a viable business model sank Logology; helping must be paired with a good business.
principles.quote: we mostly focus on like how can we help people who don't have money get a good logo instead of like how can we build a good business so that's one of the reasons we failed

principles.text: A stale product scares buyers; an outdated course kills sales, so update it.
principles.quote: it's obvious that the course hasn't been updated in a year so it's kind of like scary to people

principles.text: Full-time indie work forces you to make it work but is stressful; a paycheck gives stability.
principles.quote: I knew I will be forced to make it work so I had some savings and I'm like okay I have to make it work within that that was very helpful and at the same time incredibly stressful
